newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain surprises with interest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain surprises with interest rate rise.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke ordered a shock increase in official interest rates on Wednesday, confounding financial markets which had predicted he would not risk such a bold move ahead of a general election.
At his monthly monetary meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George, Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, authorised an immediate rise in interest rates to 6.0 percent from 5.75 percent.
The central bank had been pressing since June for a tightening in monetary policy, arguing that rising economic growth meant there was a risk of a resurgence in inflation within the next two years.

Clarke, conscious that higher rates could undermine the popularity of the already embattled Conservative government by making home loans more expensive for millions of home-owners, resisted the bank's advice for several months.
But on Wednesday he agreed to raise rates for the first time since February 1995, saying he was determined to take no risks with inflation.
"The economy is performing exceptionally well," Clarke said.

"However, the strength of activity indicates that a rise in rates is desirable if we are to deliver our inflation target of 2.5 percent or less in the medium term. Experience has shown that by increasing rates early, as I did in 1994 and I am doing today, possible inflation can be nipped in the bud."
Welcoming the decision, George said: "Moving now to moderate the accelerating pace of the economic upswing is likely to mean that we will need to tighten policy by less than we would otherwise."
Underlying annual inflation has stuck stubbornly above the government's 2.5 percent target. It was 2.9 percent in September.
London financial markets, which had seen Clarke cut interest rates four times since last December, were caught off guard by Wednesday's increase.
The pound sterling surged to a 22-month high against the mark and a 19-month high against the dollar, while share prices and government bonds fell back.
Commercial banks raised their own base lending rates but major mortgage lenders said they had no immediate plans to increase the cost of home loans.
Economists said that although Clarke might be perceived to have caved in to pressure from the Bank of England, the rate rise would probably enhance his reputation as a prudent finance minister.
"Clarke has now demonstrated he is prepared to raise rates in the face of political flak," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, who said further rate increases could follow.

"The tightening has come well ahead of our expectations and must be good news for the credibility of the government's anti-inflation policy," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank of America.
The opposition Labour Party, which has a strong opinion poll lead over the Conservatives ahead of an election due by next May, said the rate rise illustrated the underlying weakness of the economy.

"It shows that the economic policies of the last 17 years have failed to deliver strength in the British economy that can enable us to grow without hitting inflation," shadow finance spokesman Gordon Brown told BBC television.

But Clarke predicted that the Conservatives would still be in power in two years' time, when he said the fruits of Wednesday's decision would be apparent in the form of steady, non-inflationary economic growth.
